precautions: Improve drainage in the plantation
Remove and burn fallen infected nuts
Avoid overhead irrigation during monsoon
dosage: Spray 1% Bordeaux mixture on bunches at onset of monsoon
Repeat spray after 40 days if rainfall is heavy
notes: Caused by Phytophthora fungus; timing the first spray just before monsoon onset is more effective than spraying after symptoms appear.

precautions: Use disease-free planting material
Maintain balanced fertilization
Isolate and rogue severely affected palms
dosage: No direct chemical cure available
Manage suspected insect vectors with recommended systemic insecticide
notes: A phytoplasma disease with no curative treatment - management is preventive and vector-control focused. Consult a local agricultural extension officer.

precautions: Ensure good field drainage
Avoid injury to the crown region during intercultural operations
dosage: Remove and destroy affected bud tissue
Apply Bordeaux paste to the wound after removal
notes: Caught early (before the spindle leaf collapses), palms can often be saved. Affects both arecanut and coconut.

precautions: Prune for good air circulation
Avoid overhead irrigation
Remove and destroy infected plant debris
dosage: Spray Copper oxychloride (0.3%) at 15-day intervals during flowering/fruiting
Alternate with Carbendazim if resistance is suspected
notes: One of the most common fungal diseases across many crops; early-season preventive spraying is more effective than treating visible lesions.

precautions: Avoid water stress and overhead irrigation
Harvest promptly to avoid overripe fruit on the plant
dosage: Spray Carbendazim (0.1%) or Copper oxychloride (0.3%) at fruit-set stage
Repeat every 10-15 days in humid conditions
notes: Particularly aggressive on chilli, okra, and papaya in warm, humid conditions - post-harvest handling matters as much as field spraying.

precautions: Avoid dense planting/overcrowding
Ensure adequate sunlight exposure
dosage: Spray Wettable sulfur (0.2%) at first sign of white powdery patches
Avoid sulfur spray in very high temperatures - can scorch leaves
notes: A very common fungal disease across many crops (cashew, chilli, papaya, okra, cucumber, cabbage relatives, marigold, rose) - the same basic treatment works across most of them.

precautions: Monitor flush and flowering stages closely - highest-risk periods
Maintain field hygiene, remove alternate host weeds nearby
dosage: Spray a recommended systemic insecticide (e.g. Imidacloprid) at early flush stage
Repeat as per product label during flowering
notes: Technically a pest, not a disease, but a major cashew yield-loss factor - included here since it presents visually similar to disease damage.

precautions: Practice crop rotation - avoid planting tomato/potato in the same spot yearly
Stake plants to improve airflow
Remove lower infected leaves promptly
dosage: Spray Mancozeb (0.25%) at 10-day intervals
Begin spraying preventively once fruiting starts in high-risk seasons
notes: Favored by warm, humid weather with intermittent dry spells. Affects both tomato and potato.

precautions: Use resistant/tolerant varieties where available
Avoid overhead irrigation, especially in the evening
Destroy volunteer potato/tomato plants nearby
dosage: Spray Copper oxychloride (0.3%) or Metalaxyl+Mancozeb combination at first sign
Spray preventively before/during cool, wet weather
notes: Can destroy a crop within days in favorable (cool, wet) conditions. Affects both tomato and potato.

precautions: Use resistant rootstock/varieties where available
Practice long crop rotation (3-4 years) with non-host crops
Avoid working in fields when plants are wet
dosage: No effective chemical cure once infected
Remove and destroy infected plants immediately to slow spread
notes: Soil-borne and highly persistent - affects tomato, brinjal, and ginger. Prevention through rotation and resistant varieties matters far more than any in-season treatment.

precautions: Use certified disease-free seed
Avoid overhead irrigation
Practice 2-3 year crop rotation with non-cruciferous crops
dosage: Spray Copper oxychloride (0.3%) at first sign of V-shaped yellow lesions
Remove and destroy infected plant debris after harvest
notes: Bacterial disease affecting cabbage and related crops - spreads rapidly in warm, wet weather via water splash.

precautions: Raise soil pH above 7.2 with lime application if clubroot-prone
Improve field drainage
Avoid moving infected soil/tools between fields
dosage: No curative chemical treatment - focus on prevention
Soil fumigation is an option for severe, persistent infestations (specialist consultation recommended)
notes: A soil-borne pathogen that can persist in soil for years - affects cabbage and radish. Field-level prevention is the only practical management for a small farm.

precautions: Improve air circulation and avoid waterlogging
Avoid overhead irrigation, water early in the day if needed
dosage: Spray Metalaxyl + Mancozeb (0.25%) at first sign of yellow patches with grey fungal growth underneath
Repeat at 10-day intervals in humid weather
notes: Distinct from powdery mildew - look for fuzzy grey/purple growth on the underside of leaves. Affects cabbage, radish, onion, and cucumber.

precautions: Control whitefly vector population with yellow sticky traps
Remove and destroy infected plants promptly to reduce virus reservoir
Use virus-free, certified seedlings
dosage: No direct chemical cure for the virus itself
Spray recommended insecticide against whitefly vector (e.g. Imidacloprid) to slow spread
notes: Transmitted by whiteflies - managing the insect vector is the only practical control, not the virus directly.

precautions: Improve soil drainage, avoid waterlogging
Avoid overwatering, especially in heavy soils
Use well-draining potting mix for container plants
dosage: Drench soil with Trichoderma-based biofungicide as a preventive measure
For active infection, drench with Copper oxychloride (0.3%) and reduce watering frequency
notes: Almost always linked to overwatering or poor drainage rather than the pathogen alone. Affects marigold and carrot among others.

precautions: Remove spent flowers and blighted plant material promptly
Avoid overhead watering and overcrowded planting
Ensure good air circulation
dosage: Spray a recommended fungicide (e.g. Mancozeb) at first sign of grey fuzzy mould
Remove and destroy affected blooms immediately
notes: Thrives in cool, humid, poorly-ventilated conditions - often called 'grey mould'.

precautions: Avoid overhead watering - water at the base of the plant
Remove and destroy fallen infected leaves
Prune for good air circulation
dosage: Spray Mancozeb or Copper-based fungicide at 10-14 day intervals during humid weather
Begin preventive spraying at the start of the growing season in high-risk areas
notes: The most common rose disease - persistent leaf removal (sanitation) is as important as spraying.

precautions: Prune and destroy affected branches well below the visibly infected area
Disinfect pruning tools between cuts
Avoid water stress
dosage: Apply Bordeaux paste to pruning wounds and cut surfaces
Spray Copper oxychloride (0.3%) on the plant after pruning
notes: Often enters through pruning wounds or winter damage - clean pruning technique is a major preventive factor.

precautions: Use disease-free tissue-culture planting material
Avoid moving soil/water between infected and clean fields
Improve field drainage
dosage: No effective chemical cure - Fusarium persists in soil for decades
Remove and destroy infected plants, avoid replanting bananas in the same spot
notes: Also called Fusarium wilt - one of the most destructive banana diseases worldwide, entirely soil-borne with no cure.

precautions: Remove and destroy heavily infected leaves (de-leafing)
Improve plant spacing for airflow
Avoid excess nitrogen fertilization
dosage: Spray Propiconazole or Mancozeb-based fungicide at 3-4 week intervals in high-risk season
Rotate fungicide types to avoid resistance build-up
notes: A major banana leaf disease that reduces photosynthetic area and yield - persistent fungicide rotation is standard commercial practice.

precautions: Use only certified virus-free planting material (tissue culture)
Control the banana aphid vector
Remove and destroy infected plants immediately including the corm
dosage: No chemical cure for the virus
Spray recommended insecticide to control the aphid vector
notes: One of the most serious banana viral diseases - infected plants should be uprooted and destroyed, not just cut back, since the corm remains infectious.

precautions: Use certified disease-free seed
Avoid overhead irrigation
Practice crop rotation with non-solanaceous crops
dosage: Spray Mancozeb (0.25%) at 10-day intervals starting from early growth stage
Remove and destroy infected fruit and plant debris
notes: Affects brinjal fruit and stems - can cause significant post-harvest fruit rot if not managed in the field.

precautions: Control aphid vector population
Remove and destroy infected plants promptly
Avoid planting near other cucurbit/papaya crops with known infection
dosage: No chemical cure for the virus itself
Manage aphid vectors with recommended insecticide to slow spread
notes: One of the most economically damaging papaya diseases globally - aphid-transmitted, so vector control is the main practical management.

precautions: Use rust-resistant coffee varieties where available
Maintain proper shade levels - both too much and too little shade increase risk
Ensure balanced fertilization
dosage: Spray Copper oxychloride (0.3%) preventively before monsoon
Systemic fungicides (e.g. Triadimefon) can be used for established infections per label directions
notes: A historically devastating disease that reshaped global coffee production (it wiped out Sri Lanka's coffee industry in the 1800s) - preventive spraying before the rainy season is standard practice.

precautions: Prune for good air circulation
Harvest ripe berries promptly
Remove and destroy infected berries and mummified fruit
dosage: Spray Copper-based fungicide at flowering and again at pinhead berry stage
Repeat during wet weather through berry development
notes: Causes direct crop loss by rotting berries rather than just damaging leaves - timing sprays to flowering/fruit-set stages is critical.

precautions: Avoid overhead irrigation
Ensure good field drainage and spacing
Remove and destroy infected leaves
dosage: Spray Metalaxyl + Mancozeb (0.25%) at first sign of white pustules on leaf undersides
Repeat at 10-day intervals in cool, humid weather
notes: Common on radish and other cruciferous vegetables in cool, humid conditions.

precautions: Maintain balanced fertilization, particularly potassium
Improve drainage in low-lying coconut plots
Remove and destroy severely affected palms to reduce spread
dosage: No curative chemical treatment - management is nutritional and cultural
Apply recommended balanced fertilizer schedule to improve palm tolerance
notes: A phytoplasma-associated coconut disease endemic to parts of southern India - management is long-term and cultural, not a quick fix.

precautions: Improve drainage around the base of the palm
Avoid mechanical injury to the crown
Remove and destroy severely rotted leaves
dosage: Apply Bordeaux paste to affected leaf bases
Spray Copper oxychloride (0.3%) on the crown region during monsoon
notes: Often appears alongside root wilt disease in coconut, worsened by waterlogging and poor drainage.

precautions: Maintain soil pH below 5.5 where scab-prone (scab thrives in alkaline soil)
Avoid excess lime application
Ensure even soil moisture during tuber formation
dosage: No curative treatment for tubers already infected
Choose scab-resistant potato varieties for future planting in affected soil
notes: A cosmetic/quality issue more than a yield-killer - management is almost entirely about soil pH and moisture, not spraying.

precautions: Avoid overhead irrigation
Ensure good field drainage and plant spacing
Remove and destroy infected leaves
dosage: Spray Mancozeb (0.25%) at 10-day intervals during humid weather
Begin preventive spraying if extended wet weather is forecast
notes: A major onion foliar disease - purple-brown lesions with concentric rings are the identifying symptom.

precautions: Use certified disease-free sets/seedlings
Avoid injury to bulbs during harvest and handling
Improve field drainage
dosage: No curative treatment once bulbs are infected
Discard infected bulbs at harvest to prevent storage spread
notes: Primarily a storage and post-harvest concern for onion - prevention at planting and careful harvest handling matter more than any spray.

precautions: Control whitefly vector with yellow sticky traps
Remove and destroy infected plants promptly
Use resistant/tolerant okra varieties where available
dosage: No direct chemical cure for the virus
Spray recommended insecticide against whitefly vector to slow spread
notes: One of the most common and damaging okra diseases in India - whitefly management is the primary practical control.

precautions: Avoid overhead irrigation
Ensure good plant spacing for airflow
Remove and destroy infected plant debris after harvest
dosage: Spray Wettable sulfur (0.2%) or Mancozeb at first sign of orange-brown pustules
Repeat at 10-14 day intervals in humid weather
notes: Common on French beans - orange-brown pustules on leaf undersides are the identifying symptom.

precautions: Use certified disease-free seed
Avoid working in fields when plants are wet
Practice crop rotation with non-host crops
dosage: Spray Copper oxychloride (0.3%) at first sign of water-soaked lesions
Remove and destroy infected plant debris after harvest
notes: Spreads rapidly via water splash and contaminated tools - avoiding field work on wet plants meaningfully reduces spread.

precautions: Control aphid vector population
Remove and destroy infected plants promptly
Disinfect tools between plants when handling suspected infections
dosage: No chemical cure for the virus itself
Manage aphid vectors with recommended insecticide to slow spread
notes: Common on cucumber and other cucurbits - mottled yellow-green leaf pattern is the identifying symptom.

precautions: Avoid overhead irrigation
Ensure good field drainage and plant spacing
Remove and destroy infected foliage after harvest
dosage: Spray Mancozeb (0.25%) at 10-day intervals during humid weather
Begin preventive spraying if extended wet weather is forecast
notes: Common on carrot foliage - can reduce yield by weakening the plant even without directly damaging the root.

precautions: Improve drainage around vine base
Avoid waterlogging, especially during monsoon
Use disease-free planting material
dosage: Drench soil with Copper oxychloride (0.3%) or Metalaxyl-based fungicide around affected vines
Remove and destroy severely wilted vines to prevent spread
notes: Also called Phytophthora foot rot - the most serious black pepper disease, can kill a vine within days in waterlogged conditions.

precautions: Improve soil drainage and organic matter content
Avoid nematode-infested planting material
Maintain balanced fertilization
dosage: Apply nematicide if root-knot nematodes are confirmed as a contributing factor
No single quick chemical fix - focus on overall vine health and soil condition
notes: A slower-progressing decline than quick wilt, often linked to a combination of fungal pathogens, nematodes, and poor soil health.

precautions: Use disease-free, treated rhizomes for planting
Ensure good field drainage - both ginger and turmeric are highly sensitive to waterlogging
Practice crop rotation
dosage: Treat seed rhizomes with a recommended fungicide (e.g. Mancozeb) before planting
Drench soil with Copper oxychloride (0.3%) at first sign of yellowing/wilting
notes: The single most damaging ginger disease - most losses trace back to poor drainage rather than the pathogen itself.

precautions: Avoid overhead irrigation
Ensure good field drainage and plant spacing
Remove and destroy infected foliage
dosage: Spray Mancozeb (0.25%) or Copper oxychloride (0.3%) at 10-14 day intervals during humid weather
notes: A generic fungal leaf disease name used across several crops including ginger - specific pathogen identification helps if the standard spray doesn't improve symptoms within 2-3 applications.
